description: Explains the nature and behaviour of light, including luminous and non-luminous objects, transparent, translucent and opaque materials, reflection, refraction and dispersion, mirrors, and optical instruments such as microscopes, telescopes, cameras and periscopes.

mcq.questionText: An object that produces its own light is called a:
mcq.explanation: An object producing its own light is called a luminous object. Exam Tip: The Sun and a candle flame are luminous. The Moon is non-luminous - it reflects sunlight.
Light travels in straight lines, known as rectilinear propagation. Exam Tip: This straight-line travel explains shadows, eclipses and pinhole cameras.

mcq.questionText: A material that allows light to pass through it clearly, so objects can be seen distinctly, is called:
mcq.explanation: Clear glass and water let light through with a clear view, making them transparent. Exam Tip: Transparent = clear view; translucent = blurry view; opaque = no light through.

mcq.questionText: A material that does NOT allow any light to pass through it is called:
mcq.explanation: No light passes through an opaque material at all. Exam Tip: Opaque materials (wood, metal, brick) block all light and cast sharp shadows.

mcq.questionText: The bouncing back of light when it hits a surface is called:
mcq.explanation: Light bouncing back off a surface is called reflection. Exam Tip: Reflection lets us see objects and is the basis of how mirrors work.

mcq.questionText: The bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another (e.g. from air into water) is called:
mcq.explanation: The bending of light as it passes between two transparent media is called refraction. Exam Tip: Refraction makes a straw look bent in a glass of water.

mcq.questionText: The splitting of white light into its component colours, as seen in a rainbow, is called:
mcq.explanation: Splitting white light into its component colours is called dispersion. Exam Tip: A prism disperses white light into a spectrum: ROYGBIV.

mcq.questionText: In a plane mirror, the image formed is:

options.text: Virtual, upright and the same size as the object

mcq.explanation: A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual (cannot be caught on a screen), upright, and the same size as the object. Exam Tip: Plane mirror image: virtual, upright, laterally inverted, same size, same distance behind as object in front.

mcq.questionText: A curved mirror that curves inward, like the inside of a spoon, is called a:
mcq.explanation: A mirror that curves inward, like the inside of a spoon, is a concave mirror. Exam Tip: "Concave = cave" (curves inward). Used in torches, headlights, shaving mirrors.

mcq.questionText: A curved mirror that curves outward, like the back of a spoon, is called a:
mcq.explanation: A mirror that curves outward, like the back of a spoon, is a convex mirror. Exam Tip: Convex mirrors give a wide field of view - used as car side mirrors.

mcq.questionText: Which optical instrument uses lenses to magnify very small objects such as cells?
mcq.explanation: A microscope uses lenses to magnify very small, nearby objects such as cells. Exam Tip: Microscope = small, near objects; telescope = distant, large objects.

mcq.questionText: Which optical instrument is used to view distant objects such as stars and planets?
mcq.explanation: A telescope collects light from far away and magnifies distant objects such as stars and planets. Exam Tip: Telescope = far away; microscope = very close and small.

mcq.questionText: A camera forms an image on its film or sensor that is:
mcq.explanation: A camera lens focuses light to form a real (capturable), upside-down image on the film or sensor. Exam Tip: A real image can be formed on a screen; a virtual image cannot.
White light is a mixture of seven colours, as shown when it passes through a prism. Exam Tip: ROYGBIV: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

mcq.questionText: A periscope, used to see over obstacles (e.g. in a submarine), works using two:
mcq.explanation: A periscope uses two plane mirrors set at 45 degrees to reflect light twice, allowing a view over obstacles. Exam Tip: Two plane mirrors at 45 degrees let you see over a wall or above water level.

fib.questionText: An object that produces its own light is called a ____ object.
fib.explanation: An object producing its own light is luminous, unlike a non-luminous object which only reflects light. Exam Tip: The Sun and a burning candle are luminous; the Moon is not.
Light travels in straight lines, called rectilinear propagation. Exam Tip: Rectilinear propagation of light - explains shadow formation.

fib.questionText: A material that allows a clear view of objects through it is called ____.
fib.explanation: A material giving a clear view of objects through it is transparent. Exam Tip: Clear glass and clean water are transparent.

fib.questionText: The bouncing back of light from a surface is called ____.
fib.explanation: Light bouncing back from a surface is reflection. Exam Tip: Reflection lets mirrors and shiny surfaces show images.

fib.questionText: The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another is called ____.
fib.explanation: The bending of light as it passes between two media is refraction. Exam Tip: Refraction makes objects in water appear displaced.

fib.questionText: The splitting of white light into its component colours is called ____.
fib.explanation: Splitting white light into its component colours is dispersion. Exam Tip: A prism disperses white light into a spectrum.

fib.questionText: A mirror that curves inward like the inside of a spoon is called a ____ mirror.
fib.explanation: A mirror curving inward like the inside of a spoon is a concave mirror. Exam Tip: Concave mirrors are used in torches and headlights to focus light.

fib.questionText: A mirror that curves outward like the back of a spoon is called a ____ mirror.
fib.explanation: A mirror curving outward like the back of a spoon is a convex mirror. Exam Tip: Convex mirrors give a wide field of view (car mirrors).

fib.questionText: The image formed in a plane mirror is ____ (real/virtual).
fib.explanation: A plane mirror forms a virtual image that cannot be caught on a screen. Exam Tip: Virtual images cannot be projected on a screen.

fib.questionText: The optical instrument used to magnify very small, nearby objects such as cells is the ____.
fib.explanation: The microscope uses lenses to magnify very small, nearby objects such as cells. Exam Tip: Microscope for small/near; telescope for large/distant.

tf.explanation: Light travels in straight lines, a property called rectilinear propagation. Exam Tip: This explains sharp shadows from opaque objects.

tf.questionText: An opaque object allows all light to pass through it.
tf.explanation: An opaque object allows no light to pass through it at all. Exam Tip: Opaque = no light through.

tf.questionText: Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface.
tf.explanation: This is the correct definition of reflection. Exam Tip: Mirrors and shiny surfaces reflect light well.

tf.questionText: Refraction is the splitting of white light into its component colours.
tf.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light between media; dispersion is the splitting into colours. Exam Tip: Refraction = bending; dispersion = splitting into colours.

tf.questionText: The image in a plane mirror is the same size as the object.
tf.explanation: A plane mirror image is always the same size as the object. Exam Tip: The image is also as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

tf.questionText: A concave mirror curves outward like the back of a spoon.
tf.explanation: A concave mirror curves inward; it is the convex mirror that curves outward. Exam Tip: Concave = inward; convex = outward.

tf.questionText: White light is made up of seven colours.
tf.explanation: White light is a mixture of seven colours revealed by a prism. Exam Tip: A prism separates white light into these seven colours.

tf.questionText: A telescope is used to view very small, nearby objects such as cells.
tf.explanation: A telescope views distant objects, while a microscope views small, nearby objects. Exam Tip: Telescope = far; microscope = small/near.

tf.questionText: A camera forms a real, inverted image on its film or sensor.
tf.explanation: The camera lens focuses light rays to form a real, inverted image. Exam Tip: The camera lens focuses light rays to form this real image.

tf.questionText: A periscope uses two plane mirrors to allow viewing over an obstacle.
tf.explanation: A periscope uses two plane mirrors set at 45 degrees to redirect light over an obstacle. Exam Tip: Submarines use periscopes built this way.

summary.correctAnswer: A luminous object produces its own light (e.g. the Sun, a candle), while a non-luminous object does not produce light but can be seen because it reflects light from a luminous source (e.g. the Moon).
summary.explanation: This distinction explains why some objects glow on their own and others only appear lit because they reflect light. Exam Tip: The Moon is a classic non-luminous object - it only shines because it reflects sunlight.

summary.correctAnswer: Transparent materials let light through clearly (clear glass, water); translucent materials let some light through but scatter it so objects appear blurry (frosted glass); opaque materials block all light (wood, metal).
summary.explanation: The three terms describe how much light passes through a material and how clearly objects can be seen through it. Exam Tip: Transparent = clear view; translucent = blurry view; opaque = no light through.

summary.correctAnswer: The bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface, without the light passing into the material.
summary.explanation: Reflection is what allows mirrors and shiny surfaces to form images that we can see. Exam Tip: Reflection lets us see objects and is the basis of how mirrors work.

summary.correctAnswer: The bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another of different density, such as from air into water.
summary.explanation: Refraction occurs because light changes speed when it enters a different medium, causing it to bend. Exam Tip: Refraction makes a straw look bent in a glass of water.

summary.correctAnswer: The splitting of white light into its seven component colours (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet) as it passes through a prism.
summary.explanation: Dispersion happens because each colour of light bends by a slightly different amount when refracted. Exam Tip: Remember the spectrum with ROYGBIV, as seen in a rainbow.

summary.correctAnswer: A virtual, upright image that is the same size as the object and appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, but laterally inverted.
summary.explanation: Because the image cannot be projected on a screen, it is called virtual rather than real. Exam Tip: Plane mirror image: virtual, upright, laterally inverted, same size, same distance behind as object in front.

summary.correctAnswer: A concave mirror curves inward like the inside of a spoon and can magnify or focus light (used in torches and shaving mirrors); a convex mirror curves outward like the back of a spoon and gives a wide field of view with a smaller image (used in car side mirrors).
summary.explanation: The direction of curvature determines whether the mirror focuses light inward or spreads the view outward. Exam Tip: "Concave = cave" (curves inward, can magnify); convex curves outward and gives a wide view.

summary.correctAnswer: A microscope uses lenses to magnify very small, nearby objects such as cells, while a telescope uses lenses (or mirrors) to magnify distant objects such as stars and planets.
summary.explanation: Both instruments use lenses to magnify, but they are designed for opposite distance ranges. Exam Tip: Microscope = small, near objects; telescope = distant, large objects.

summary.correctAnswer: A real, inverted (upside-down) image formed on the film or sensor when the camera lens focuses light from an object.
summary.explanation: Because the image can be captured on the film or sensor, it is real rather than virtual. Exam Tip: A real image can be formed on a screen or sensor; a virtual image cannot.

summary.correctAnswer: An optical device, such as one used in a submarine, that uses two plane mirrors set at 45 degrees to reflect light twice so a viewer can see over or around an obstacle.
summary.explanation: The two mirrors redirect the light path so the eye can see objects that would otherwise be blocked from view. Exam Tip: Two plane mirrors at 45 degrees let you see over a wall or above water level.

hoq.questionText: A student shines white light through a glass prism and observes a band of colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Explain and name the phenomenon.

options.text: The light was reflected; this is reflection
The prism split the white light into its component colours; this is dispersion
The light was absorbed completely; nothing is seen
The prism created new colours from nothing

hoq.explanation: White light bends by different amounts for each colour as it passes through the prism, separating into a band of colours - this is dispersion. Exam Tip: This is exactly how a rainbow forms - raindrops act like tiny prisms.

hoq.questionText: Mirror P gives an upright, reduced image and a wide field of view (car side mirror). Mirror Q gives an enlarged, upright image when the object is close (shaving/make-up). Identify P and Q.
hoq.explanation: A wide field of view with a reduced image identifies mirror P as convex, while an enlarged image at close range identifies mirror Q as concave. Exam Tip: Convex mirrors always shrink but show a wide view. Concave mirrors magnify when close.

hoq.questionText: A pencil in a glass of water appears bent and shorter when viewed from the side. Explain using a property of light.

options.text: The pencil physically bends in water
Light from the pencil refracts (bends) as it passes from water into air, making the pencil appear bent and displaced (shorter) to the eye
The water reflects the pencil only
Light does not travel through water

hoq.explanation: The pencil does not physically bend; light travelling from the water into air refracts, displacing the apparent position of the submerged part and making the pencil look bent and shorter. Exam Tip: The pencil is straight in reality; what "bends" is the light reaching your eye, not the pencil.
